02 · Quantification

Detection probability curve, protein roll-up, detection filter, normalisation

Half of a DIA matrix is empty, and not at random: faint precursors go missing more often than bright ones. dpc() fits that as a curve, and dpcQuant() uses it to give every protein a value in every sample without imputing anything. This stage is the limpa vignette’s own sequence, unaltered.

The missingness relationship

plotAveVsMis(y)

A downward trend means detection depends on intensity and the DPC has something to fit. A flat cloud would mean missingness is closer to random, where limpa still works but gains less over simpler methods.

The curve

dpcest <- dpc(y$E)
dpcest_on <- dpcON(y$E, robust = TRUE)
plotDPC(dpcest)
dpc_parameters <- tibble(
  estimator = c("complete normal", "observed normal"),
  intercept = c(dpcest$dpc[1], dpcest_on$dpc[1]),
  slope = c(dpcest$dpc[2], dpcest_on$dpc[2])
)
dpc_parameters
estimator intercept slope
complete normal -8.958339 0.4883639
observed normal -4.856876 0.2421199

dpc() defaults to model = "cn" and its help says it then returns dpcCN(), the complete-normal estimator the limpa FAQ recommends for noisy data. Its subset = 2000 default fits on a systematic sample stratified by missingness and mean intensity rather than all 47,133 rows. limpa documents robust as “Only used if `model=‘on’”, so it does nothing here and the subsample supplies the robustness.

We report the slope as fitted and never substitute a preset. The FAQ puts the usable range at 0.1 to 1.0 and calls 0.7 to 0.9 typical for DIA-NN searched with match-between-runs. The vignette adds that the slope comes out low when peptides vary a lot, which is what a within-subject design with heavy missingness looks like. limpa’s own published DIA-NN case study fitted 0.59 and used it. A shallow slope also recovers less from missing values, so it errs toward finding nothing rather than finding too much.

Note

The visual fit is not the diagnostic. plotDPC() draws a curve in unobserved intensity against proportions computed on observed intensity, so some discrepancy is structural. Judge the slope.

Roll-up

dpcQuant() fits an additive precursor-plus-sample model per protein, maximising a posterior that scores observed values by squared residual and missing values by their DPC probability. The returned $other$standard.error is why this project uses limpa: dpcDE() reads it as a precision weight, so a protein reconstructed largely from missing precursors gets a value and a wide one. Handing $E to lmFit() discards that and treats every protein as equally reliable.

elapsed <- system.time(
  proteins <- dpcQuant(y, "Protein.Group", dpc = dpcest)
)
Estimating hyperparameters ...
Quantifying proteins ...
Proteins: 1000  Precursors: 16779 (35%)
Proteins: 2000  Precursors: 31087 (65%)
Proteins: 3000  Precursors: 43037 (91%)
Proteins: 3451  Precursors: 47133 (100%)

3,451 protein groups from 47,133 precursors in 115.8 minutes. The matrix has no missing values; what varies is how certain each value is.

Detection filter

filterByDetection()’s help fixes the order: it runs after dpcQuant() and before DE, and it returns a logical vector rather than an object. For a small experiment the help suggests setting n.samples to the smallest group size. Here that is BFR_T2 with 32 samples, one short because nobody acquired S06’s left leg at T2.

The function does not read group. It counts detections across all samples and keeps a protein when that count clears the threshold, so the smallest group size sets a cohort-wide bar rather than guaranteeing detection within any one group.

group_sizes <- table(proteins$targets$group)
keep <- filterByDetection(proteins, n.samples = min(group_sizes))
proteins <- proteins[keep, ]

group_sizes

 BFR_T1  BFR_T2 HLRT_T1 HLRT_T2 
     33      32      33      33 
c(before = length(keep), kept = sum(keep), dropped = sum(!keep))
 before    kept dropped 
   3451    3042     409

Normalisation

limpa places normalisation after dpcQuant() and before dpcDE() and performs none itself, because DIA-NN has usually normalised the precursors already. What matters is which kind is needed. Comparing a sample against the average of all samples gives a difference per protein; fitting that against abundance gives a curve. A flat curve means the sample disagrees by a constant, which a per-sample shift corrects. A curve that travels means the disagreement depends on abundance, and only cyclic loess corrects that.

Here the curve travels 0.45 log2 in the median sample against 0.13 for the spread in per-sample medians, and the curvature is unrelated to treatment or timepoint.

ma_width <- function(E) {
  a <- rowMeans(E)
  apply(E, 2, \(x) diff(range(lowess(a, x - a, f = 0.5)$y)))
}

before <- median(ma_width(proteins$E))
proteins$E <- normalizeBetweenArrays(proteins$E, method = "cyclicloess")

c(before = round(before, 3), after = round(median(ma_width(proteins$E)), 3))
before  after 
 0.447  0.173

proteins.rds is written after this, so it is the matrix the model is fitted to.

What survives

protein_quality <- tibble(
  protein = rownames(proteins),
  gene = proteins$genes$Genes,
  n_precursors = proteins$genes$NPrec,
  prop_observed = proteins$genes$PropObs,
  mean_log2 = rowMeans(proteins$E),
  mean_standard_error = rowMeans(proteins$other$standard.error),
  mean_n_observations = rowMeans(proteins$other$n.observations)
)
summary(protein_quality[c("mean_log2", "mean_standard_error", "prop_observed")])
   mean_log2     mean_standard_error prop_observed    
 Min.   :12.97   Min.   :0.02786     Min.   :0.03716  
 1st Qu.:16.30   1st Qu.:0.29963     1st Qu.:0.30245  
 Median :17.41   Median :0.45552     Median :0.42324  
 Mean   :17.78   Mean   :0.53157     Mean   :0.43278  
 3rd Qu.:18.96   3rd Qu.:0.73995     3rd Qu.:0.54962  
 Max.   :26.95   Max.   :1.25430     Max.   :0.97710

NPrec is what the installed version writes; the help page calls it NPeptides. A protein with a high mean standard error and few observations is one whose estimate leans on the DPC rather than on data.

plotMDSUsingSEs(proteins,
  labels = proteins$targets$group,
  col = as.integer(factor(proteins$targets$group))
)

Samples are not expected to separate by group. Every participant contributes all four cells, so between-participant variation dominates the leading dimensions and the participant term in the design is what removes it. A sample sitting far from everything else is worth investigating; a lack of group structure is not.
